to maintaining health. 
Sharp barriers between research and clinical care obstruct the virtuous 
cycle of moving scientific discoveries rapidly into clinical care and bring-
ing clinical observations back to the research setting82 (Fig. 3). Learning 
healthcare systems—in which real-time data on outcomes of healthcare 
delivery are accessed and used to enhance clinical practice—can lead to 
continuous care improvement, but only if the barriers between research 
and clinical care are reduced115. For example, offering genome sequenc-
ing to all members of a healthcare system, performed in conjunction 
with research and participant engagement and provided in real time81, 
could help to assess the clinical utility of genomic information and 
may allow providers to improve disease diagnosis and management. 
System-wide implementation of such an experiment requires not only 
extensive patient and provider education, sophisticated informatics 
capabilities, and genomics-based clinical decision support, but also the 
development and evaluation of data security and privacy protections 
to ensure patient confidentiality116. Patients should be engaged in the 
design of such systems and informed at entry to them (and periodically 
thereafter), so as to be fully aware of the nature of the ongoing research 
with their clinical data and the goals and potential risks of their participa-
tion117. Extending such studies across many healthcare systems should 
reveal common challenges and solutions118,119, thereby enhancing the 
learning healthcare model for genomic medicine more broadly (Fig. 3). 
Concluding thoughts 
The dawn of genomics featured the launch of the Human Genome Pro-
ject in October 19901. Three decades later, the field has seen stunning 
technological advances and high-profile programmatic successes, 
which in turn have led to the widespread infusion of genomic meth-
ods and approaches across the life sciences and, increasingly, into 
medicine and society. 
NHGRI has for the third time15,16 since the Human Genome Project 
undergone an extensive horizon-scanning process to capture, syn-
thesize, and articulate the most compelling strategic opportunities 
for the next phase of genomics—with particular attention to elements 
that are most relevant to human health. The now near-ubiquitous 
nature of genomics (including in the complex healthcare ecosystem) 
presented practical challenges for attaining a holistic assessment of 
the field. Another reality was that the NHGRI investment in genomics 
has now been multiplied many-fold by the seeding of human genomics 
throughout the broader research community. These changes reflect 
a continued maturation of both the field (in general) and NHGRI 
(more specifically), nicely aligning with the institute’s evolving leader-
ship role at The Forefront of Genomics. 
Embracing that role, NHGRI formulated the strategic vision described 
here, which provides an optimistic outlook that the successes in human 
genomics over the past three decades will be amplified in the coming 
decade. Many of the details about what is needed to fulfil the promise of 
genomics have now come into focus. Major unsolved problems remain— 
among them determining the role for the vast majority of functional ele-
ments in the human genome (especially those outside of protein-coding 
regions), understanding the full spectrum of genomic variation (espe-
cially that implicated in human disease), developing data-science capabili-
ties (especially those that keep pace with data generation), and improving 
healthcare through the implementation of genomic medicine (especially 
in the areas of prevention, diagnosis, and therapeutic development). 
The new decade also brings research questions related to the societal 
implications of genomics, including those related to social inequities, 
pointing to the continued importance of investigating the ethical, legal, 
and social issues related to genomics. But now more than ever, solutions 
to these problems seem to be within striking distance. T owards that end 
(and with the characteristic spirit of genomics audacity), we offer ten bold 
predictions of what might be realized in human genomics by 2030 (Box 5). 
The strategic vision articulated here was crafted on behalf of the field 
of human genomics and emphasizes broad strategic goals as opposed 
to implementation tactics. The realization of these goals will require 
further planning in conjunction with the collective creativity, ener-
gies, and resources of the global community of scientists, funders, and 
research participants. NHGRI has taken some initial steps to implement 
this vision, although these will inevitably need to be adapted as advances 
occur and circumstances change. Indeed, the final words of this strategic 
vision were formulated as the world moved urgently to deal with the 
coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (see below), providing 
a vivid reminder of the need to be nimble and the importance of nurtur-
ing all parts of the research continuum—from basic to translational to 
clinical—for protecting public health and advancing medical science. 
Despite the seismic changes seen in genomics since the inception of 
the field, the fundamental sense of curiosity, marvel, and purpose associ-
ated with genome science seems to be timeless. In concluding NHGRI’s 
previous strategic vision16—published just under a decade ago —the 
then-envisioned opportunities and challenges were provided with “ … a 
continuing sense of wonder, a continuing need for urgency, a continuing 
desire to balance ambition with reality, and a continuing responsibility

to protect individuals while maximizing the societal benefits of genom-
ics…. ” With the 2020 strategic vision described here providing a thought-
ful guide and with enduring feelings of wonder, urgency, ambition, and 
social consciousness providing unfettered momentum, we are ready 
to embark on the next exciting phase of the human genomics journey. 
Epilogue: COVID-19 and genomics 
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) 
emerged as a global threat to public health at the end of the multi-year 
process that generated the above strategic vision. Nonetheless, the 
COVID-19 pandemic provides a potent lesson about how a tiny string 
of nucleic acids can wreak global havoc on humankind. Understanding 
the mechanisms involved in the transmission of the virus, viral invasion 
and clearance, as well as the highly variable and at times disastrous 
physiological responses to infection, are fertile grounds for genom-
ics research. Genomics rapidly assumed crucial roles in COVID-19 
research and clinical care in areas such as (1) the deployment of DNA- 
and RNA-sequencing technologies for diagnostics, tracking of viral 
isolates, and environmental monitoring; (2) the use of synthetic nucleic 
acid technologies for studying SARS-CoV-2 virulence and facilitating 
vaccine development; (3) the examination of how human genomic 
variation influences infectivity, disease severity, vaccine efficacy, and 
treatment response; (4) the adherence to principles and values related 
to open science, data sharing, and consortia-based collaborations; 
and (5) the provision of genomic data science tools to study COVID-19 
pathophysiology. The growing adoption of genomic approaches and 
technologies into myriad aspects of the global response to the COVID-19 
pandemic serves as another important and highly visible example of the 
integral and vital nature of genomics in modern research and medicine.

4        NHLBI STRATEGIC VISION   |    FY 2026–2030
DIRECTOR’S MESSAGE
Transformative vision propels science and its application to advance 
health and health care, and for over 75 years, the public has entrusted 
the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) to support and 
advance research and its translation to improve lives and save lives  
for people across our nation and around the world. As a public service science institute, our 
mission is to simultaneously see over the horizon to identify future challenges and opportunities 
while discovering and applying solutions to our current and newly emergent health and public 
health challenges. 
NHLBI’s transformative vision comes from the public we serve — from people and communities 
from every walk of life who bring unique, diverse, and complementary expertise, insights, and 
lived experience to inform, inspire, and innovate. In this context, the collaborative Strategic Vision 
we first developed in 2016 catalyzed and powered advances across heart, lung, blood, and sleep 
(HLBS) science and medicine, moving the entire biomedical enterprise forward to achieve health 
and healthcare milestones that appeared as distant goals when we glimpsed them over the 
horizon 8 years ago. 
Your contributions — driven by collaborative community action — energized discovery science 
and its application to gene therapies so that in 2024, multiple U.S. Food and Drug Administration 
(FDA)-approved therapeutics now exist to ameliorate sickle cell disease, bringing hope and better 
health to the individuals and families that have so long born the burden of this transgenerational 
disorder. Similarly, our collaborative partnerships enabled our swift, agile, multifaceted, and 
ongoing responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. Discovery science provided us the tools while 
community-powered implementation efforts translated this science into action to save lives and 
improve health outcomes in every community, including those bearing the gravest burdens —  
our most underserved and high-risk populations.
Through forward-thinking collaboration with stakeholders and partners, we revisited our  
Strategic Vision to update our collective “view” over the horizon and to assess emergent 
hypersonic technological developments that are exponentially accelerating scientific  
discoveries and medical advances.

5        NHLBI STRATEGIC VISION   |    FY 2026–2030
Throughout this update, we have renewed and expanded our commitment to diverse and inclusive 
partnerships, collaborative community-based research, and the rapid translation of discovery 
science into public health improvements and frontline, personalized, point-of-care medicine. 
The updated NHLBI Strategic Vision better enables us to adapt and leverage emergent science and 
technology to redress today’s most pressing health issues, while helping us anticipate the future with 
foresight and compass points to guide our actions and facilitate our progress. Although emerging 
tools like artificial intelligence and machine learning promise to further our understanding of human 
biology and to accelerate improvements in health and health care, we remain deeply committed to 
the ethical application of all scientific and technological discoveries to ensure health for all, and to 
ameliorate health disparities, including addressing the social determinants of health (SDOH) that are 
the very foundations of good health. Well health, health promotion, disease prevention, and treatment 
are inseparable from SDOH, and some of our greatest challenges now and in the future revolve 
around whole health and the health of our environment. 
As new discoveries are made and our understanding of human biology increases, our Strategic 
Vision will continue to evolve, serving as evergreen guidance to allow us to adaptively respond 
to rapidly changing challenges, opportunities, discoveries, and resources. Fundamental biology, 
implementation science, and community partnerships have been the backbone of NHLBI’s research 
since our founding 75 years ago, and those tenets will continue to power transformative science and 
its implementation for better health and health care.
A cornerstone of our public service science is the continuous and productive engagement of a broad, 
diverse, and inclusive circle of partners. Your synergistic and complementary voices provide robust, 
resilient, and adaptive guidance enabling and empowering swift, efficient, and effective leveraging of 
unprecedented scientific opportunities to redress HLBS health challenges now and in the generations 
that follow. 
We are deeply grateful for your partnership and for your individual and collective expertise and 
input as we continue our work together to achieve better health, equitable top-tier health care, and 
effective and responsive public health that improves lives and saves lives for all people across our 
country and around our world.
Sincerely,
Gary H. Gibbons, M.D
.

RELEVANT MANDATES
In June 1948, President Harry S. Truman signed 
the National Heart Act (Public Law 80-655), which 
created and established the National Heart Institute 
(NHI). That August, Surgeon General Leonard A. 
Scheele, by General Circular No. 36, Organization 
Order No. 14, established the NHI as one of the 
Institutes at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). 
On November 10, 1969, the NHI was renamed the 
National Heart and Lung Institute (NHLI) to reflect the 
expansion of the NHI’s functions. Three years later, 
the National Heart, Blood Vessel, Lung, and Blood 
Act of 1972 (P .L. 92-423) expanded the Institute’s 
authority to advance the national response against 
heart, blood vessel, lung, and blood diseases. The act provided for intensified and coordinated 
Institute activities in accordance with a comprehensive, specified National Heart, Blood Vessel, 
Lung, and Blood Disease Program to be planned by the director and the Advisory Council.
In June 1976, Title I of the Health Research and Health Services Amendments of 1976 (P .L. 94-
278) redesignated the NHLI as the NHLBI to even further reinforce the national fight against
heart, blood vessel, lung, and blood diseases. It authorized the NHLBI to conduct research in the
use of blood and blood products and in the management of blood resources. In June 1993, the
NIH Revitalization Act of 1993 (P .L. 103-43) established the National Center on Sleep Disorders
Research (NCSDR) within the NHLBI. The NHLBI currently operates under the Research and
Investigation Section 301, U.S. Code Citation 428241; National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
Section 401(a), U.S. Code Citation 42281. The NHLBI director and the National Heart, Lung,
and Blood Advisory Council continue to plan the national program under the basic P .L. 92-423

THE BURDEN OF HEART, LUNG, BLOOD, AND SLEEP DISORDERS
Since its inception, the NHLBI community has fostered a legacy of research excellence through 
groundbreaking fundamental discovery science, landmark clinical trials and population-based 
cohort studies, and innovative health education and dissemination efforts. Despite the significant 
advances in treatment and prevention made during these decades, the chronic conditions 
resulting from HLBS diseases and disorders still pose a major health and economic burden on 
the United States. Through its broad research portfolio, the NHLBI is tasked with combating not 
only the major causes of death and disability, but also rare disorders such as sickle cell disease, 
thalassemia, and pulmonary fibrosis. Although these disorders are rare in the overall population, 
the burdens they place on those affected are enormous. Despite research advances, HLBS 
diseases and disorders continue to be among the leading causes of death and disability in the 
United States.

Investigator-initiated ideas are the principal 
way we support science, but the complex and 
nuanced nature of emerging threats to public 
health require creative solutions that help 
address problems that are complex, highly 
evolving, and that have undefined endpoints.  
This unique approach is evident in NHLBI’s 
responses to the burden of sickle cell disease 
and to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Cure Sickle Cell initiative was created by the NHLBI in 2018 to use emerging safe and 
promising genetic therapies to improve the lives of individuals living with sickle cell disease. 
This initiative actively engages the sickle cell disease community — patients, family members, 
caregivers, and advocates — to work together on a path to a cure. Cure Sickle Cell encourages 
collaboration among researchers, industry, nonprofit organizations, and policy-making agencies, 
all of whom play a role in exploring the scientific questions needed to safely and effectively 
advance potential therapies.
In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the NHLBI evolved a strategy not unlike that of the Cure 
Sickle Cell initiative. In June 2020, the NHLBI developed the Collaborating Network of Networks for 
Evaluating COVID-19 and Therapeutic Strategies (CONNECTS) initiative. This program facilitated 
collaboration between experts in pulmonary, critical care, and cardiothoracic surgeries and 
enabled the development of a master protocol for research on treatments to reduce serious 
illness and death in patients with COVID-19. In 2020, the NHLBI initiated three clinical trials that 
later became part of CONNECTS and the NIH Accelerating COVID-19 Therapeutic Interventions 
and Vaccines (ACTIV) public–private partnership. The goal was to develop a coordinated research 
strategy for prioritizing and speeding the development of the most promising treatments and 
vaccines. Known as ACTIV-4, this program investigated the efficacy of anticoagulation and 
antithrombotic therapy in reducing life-threatening thrombotic cardiovascular and pulmonary 
complications in newly diagnosed COVID-19 patients not requiring hospital admission, COVID-19 
patients hospitalized with moderate and severe disease, and patients recovering from COVID-19.

PROJECTS
The Alliance for Community 
Engagement – Partnership 
for Action Toward Health 
(ACE-PATH)
ACE-PATH seeks to empower communities cumulatively and disproportionately 
affected by social determinants of health (SDOH) and health disparities across the 
United States. Its primary goal is to maximize community engagement to achieve 
optimal health despite climate related risks. Supported community-engaged research 
projects are charged to (1) Identify, develop, and test effective community-engaged 
strategies to improve the adoption and use of specific treatments or tools to respond 
to community health challenges. (2) Support community-engaged research to enhance 
the adoption, integration, and sustainment of interventions addressing the impacts of 
local health stressors. (3) Build trust and strong partnerships with all interested 
parties to exchange knowledge and encourage implementation of promising practices 
to strengthen and improve community health. (4) Inform strategies to reduce the 
effects of prioritized local health stressors in U.S. communities.
Accelerating Medicines 
Partnership® (AMP®)
AMP® is a public–private partnership between the NIH, the U.S. Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA), multiple biopharmaceutical and life science companies, 
and nonprofit and other organizations. It aims to transform the current model for 
developing new diagnostics and treatments. Thus far (2024), AMP has supported nine 
scientific projects, one of which the NHLBI sponsors, which addresses heart failure.
Community Engagement 
Alliance (CEAL) 
CEAL’s mission is to improve health outcomes, and strengthen community 
partnerships through community-engaged research that addresses health 
disparities. The alliance includes various initiatives that promote community-engaged 
research aimed at improving the health and well-being of communities that most 
often experience health disparities. These initiatives encourage community-driven, 
intervention-based research to address disparities in the context of SDOH, as well 
as the Community Engagement Alliance Consultative Resource (CEACR), a unique 
program that provides targeted consultations to researchers looking to improve  
their community engagement and participation efforts.

Trans-Omics for Precision

NHLBI’s TOPMed contributes to NIH’s precision medicine enterprise through the 
integration of whole-genome sequencing and other omics data (e.g., metabolic 
profiles, epigenomics, protein and RNA expression patterns) with behavioral, 
imaging, environmental, and clinical data. NHLBI’s Biodata Catalyst is a cloud-based 
ecosystem that offers researchers data, analytic tools, applications, and workflows 
in secure workspaces. It increases access to NHLBI datasets and provides innovative 
data analysis capabilities to help researchers accelerate discoveries and develop 
new diagnostic tools, therapeutics, and prevention strategies.
NIH-Global Alliance for 
Chronic Diseases (GACD)

This global partnership, with NIH participation, supports implementation and 
multimorbidity research to reduce the noncommunicable disease burden in low- and

populations. This program seeks to overcome barriers to implementing evidence-

PLANNING PROCESS
Strategic visioning is a process that was 
initiated in recognition of the transformational 
scientific advances that are emerging at 
an accelerating pace. By design, the NHLBI 
Strategic Vision is a dynamic document, 
regularly updated with input from people at 
the leading edge of health and science. Many 
research goals that once seemed remote 
are now within reach, and innovative technologies have rendered mundane scientific processes 
more facile. For example, in the next decade, preventable cardiovascular disease deaths for all 
age groups could decline by more than 30 percent with greater adoption of proven prevention 
and treatment strategies. A stroke-free era for children worldwide with sickle cell disease is now 
imaginable. The NHLBI Strategic Vision is the culmination of an unprecedented effort to engage 
communities in identifying and prioritizing the most compelling science for which the NHLBI 
provides leadership. 
Over the next 5 years, these collective ideas could catalyze the closing of large gaps in knowledge 
and could break through significant barriers to research progress in adherence to the Institute’s 
enduring principles.  
This document reflects an update of the 2016 Strategic Vision, which included more than 100 
compelling questions and critical challenges that aligned with eight scientific objectives and four 
goals. For this update, the NHLBI harnessed collective inputs and community-level participation 
to highlight areas of emerging needs and scientific advancements.

The NHLBI continually assesses and monitors progress toward the previously described four 
goals and eight objectives while responding to new challenges and building on emerging 
discoveries. We recognize fully that the Strategic Vision alone is insufficient to affect change 
without meaningful oversight and implementation.

To confirm that NHLBI-funded activities remain in alignment with the Institute’s priorities, 
periodic analyses are conducted to evaluate research portfolios for potential gaps and

division engages publicly through workshops and other efforts to garner inputs and insights 
supporting the establishment priorities for science. The divisions are assessed on an ongoing

RESOURCES AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
The thoughtful and strategic stewardship of resources is crucial to the success of the NHLBI 
mission. Toward that end, rigorous oversight and guidance is applied to the sharing of data 
and biospecimens and to the accessibility and management of resources and infrastructure. 
Strengthen Biorepositories 
The NHLBI demonstrates its commitment to the responsible management of research 
investments by promoting scientific rigor and maximizing the use of data and biospecimen 
resources. We emphasize standardizing protocols and resource handling to maximize 
reproducibility. The Biologic Specimen and Data Repository Information Coordinating Center 
(BioLINCC) supports access to NHLBI-funded biospecimen and data resources and enables 
access to and maximizes the scientific value of both the biorepository and data repository. 
Promote Data Science
The NHLBI BioData Catalyst® is an innovative data ecosystem that allows researchers to  
access data, analytics tools, applications, and workflows. Investigators may access data  
in a multidimensional environment at the scale and depth that makes the data readable for 
artificial intelligence and machine learning capabilities. This groundbreaking coordination  
of datasets promotes equal access, transparency, and collaboration between scientific 
partners. It also democratizes data in a way that enables reproducibility and accelerates 
progress toward discoveries that reduce the burden of heart, lung, and blood diseases  
and sleep disorders.

Operational Priorities 
PARTNERSHIPS AND INNOVATION 
Crucial to advancing the Institute’s mission is the support, input, and insights from and 
collaborations with the many communities vested in HLBS research. Scientific advancement is 
driven through the free flow and exchange of ideas and knowledge. For the NHLBI, engagement 
and partnerships (within and beyond the NIH and the U.S. Department of Health and Human 
Services [HHS]) are foundational to the generation of scientific ideas. These exchanges occur 
between people with a range of expertise, influence, and interests, including patients and their 
families, patient advocacy groups and community organizations, local health departments, 
scientists, healthcare professionals, professional societies, and the media.
Enhance Partnerships
Research is a collaborative effort that would not be possible without the insights and support 
gained from research partners that work directly with NHLBI investigators. These have included, 
for example, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, which supports the development of affordable, 
gene-based cures for sickle cell disease and HIV, and the California Institute for Regenerative 
Medicine (CIRM), which works with the NHLBI to explore the use of innovative technologies and 
therapies. Another example is our partnership with the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation 
(IHME), which supports county-level assessments of the U.S. burden of diseases and risks. Of great 
value are the partnerships and meaningful engagements with community-based organizations 
and patient representatives who work alongside our funded investigators to achieve our research 
objectives. These engagements provide insights that expand our perspectives on approaches to 
advancing HLBS research. Having effective partnerships across our portfolio is an indispensable 
research asset. 
Promote Innovation
The Institute harnesses the creativity of individual scientists by maintaining a vigorous 
investigator-initiated research portfolio. The NHLBI Small Business Innovation Research/Small 
Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program fosters knowledge, ideas, and innovation by 
supporting research and development conducted by U.S. -owned and -operated small businesses 
that pursue commercially promising technologies to prevent, diagnose, and treat HLBS-related 
diseases and disorders.

Similarly, the NHLBI Catalyze Program, a pipeline for the development of technologies and 
products, aims to drive the discovery of new therapies and cures; support the development 
of novel predictive, diagnostic, and therapeutic products; and train a diverse and globally 
competitive biomedical workforce. This program offers a coordinated support system to 
help investigators use their product development and entrepreneurial skills for innovative 
technologies and transformative platforms.
TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY 
As part of its efforts to enhance communication and 
engagement to build trust and confidence, the NHLBI has 
supported robust programs that call for community and  
clinic interactions that uphold key values. Those values 
include implementing evidence-based science and providing

health outcomes. These programs are all targeted to ensure 
that NHLBI research reaches and benefits those who are  
most in need.
DISSEMINATION AND IMPLEMENTATION RESEARCH FOR POPULATIONS  
AND COMMUNITIES 
To ensure that research progress extends to communities, the NHLBI supports dissemination 
and implementation research programs designed to translate evidence-based practices and 
interventions into real-world settings where patients and affected communities might benefit.  
For example, the Disparities Elimination through Coordinated Interventions to Prevent and Control 
Heart and Lung Disease Risk (DECIPHeR) program — an ambitious national effort — develops, 
tests, and supports sustainable implementation of strategies that achieve health equity in the 
treatment of cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases and risks while maximizing the positive 
impact on community health. Similarly, the Heart, Lung, and Blood Co-morbidities Implementation 
Models in People Living with HIV (HLB SIMPLe) program is exploring strategies for the optimal  
and sustainable delivery of effective prevention and treatment of HLBS comorbidities in people 
living with HIV in low- and middle-income countries and Small Island Developing States.

21       NHLBI STRATEGIC VISION   |    FY 2026–2030
Programs like DECIPHeR and HLB-SIMPLe recognize the many factors associated with the 
successful implementation of evidence-based interventions and guidelines in clinical and 
community settings. This is especially the case for people in underserved populations — those  
who are part of certain racial and ethnic minority groups, who live in rural areas, and who have  
a lower socioeconomic status.
Educate Patients
The NHLBI supports several educational programs that aim to ensure patients receive evidence-
based resources that raise their awareness about HLBS health. These resources include content 
related to sleep, diet, and nutrition, as well as other lifestyle issues that transcend the NHLBI 
portfolio. NHLBI education efforts support the advancement of evidence-based diet plans, 
including the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) eating plan and the Therapeutic 
Lifestyle Changes (TLC) program, that help improve cholesterol numbers. Other programs include 
The Heart Truth®, a legacy Institute program first designed to raise awareness about heart 
disease as the leading cause of death in women but has expanded to address heart disease as the 
leading cause of death for all Americans, with special emphasis on disproportionately impacted 
communities; the Blood Diseases & Disorders Education Program, which aims to bring greater 
visibility to blood donation, blood safety, and blood diseases and disorders like anemia and sickle 
cell disease; and Learn More Breathe Better®, which promotes awareness of lung health, including 
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and other lung diseases that affect 
Americans. These programs are critical to our mandate to ensure that NHLBI research progress is 
disseminated to meet the health information needs of health and community professionals and the 
public, particularly those who might benefit the most.

22       NHLBI STRATEGIC VISION   |    FY 2026–2030
EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
By diligently establishing networks and maintaining our capacity to operate, the NHLBI can  
ensure that we are able to effectively respond to public health emergencies as they arise. 
Establish Networks
NHLBI networks were poised to respond to the nation’s research needs when the COVID-19 
pandemic hit. By April 2020, the NHLBI issued a funding opportunity as part of the trans-NIH ACTIV 
initiative. This resulted in the launch of CONNECTS in June 2020. CONNECTS built upon NHLBI’s 
existing clinical research networks across the nation and around the world to better understand 
the risk of severe illness from COVID-19. The network efficiently brought together experts from 
various fields, including pulmonary critical care physicians and cardiothoracic surgeons. These 
experts collaborated to develop a research master protocol for researching effective treatments 
that reduced serious illness and death in patients with COVID-19. The lessons learned from 
the COVID-19 pandemic will serve to ensure that the Institute remains poised to act swiftly and 
decisively for any future public health emergencies. 
Maintain Continuity of Operations
It is crucial that the NHLBI maintains plans and resources to ensure that operations to support 
HLBS health continue during a crisis. Continuity of Operations (COOP) planning enables us to 
prepare to respond during an emergency, and it ensures the execution of essential functions 
through all circumstances. COOP planning is a multilayered resource that includes COOP guides 
and multiple training programs designed to ensure the continuous execution of essential functions 
through all circumstances. 
Increase the Capacity to Operate
Recognizing that today’s infrastructure may not be best suited to respond to tomorrow’s crises, 
the NHLBI is continually working to optimize our research resources so that we remain flexible 
and adaptable in our ability to address the next public health emergency. To that end, we are 
committed to diversifying our workforce, securing our research infrastructures, accelerating  
our research, and enriching our community relationships and partnerships.

COMPELLING QUESTIONS AND CRITICAL CHALLENGES 
Compelling questions and critical challenges are conceptual tools that help us more  
deeply explore challenges and opportunities related to the goals, objectives, and  
crosscutting themes.  
• Compelling Questions are unanswered questions or poorly understood areas of
research that require broad NHLBI support because their complexity exceeds the
capacity of any one investigator-initiated program.
• Critical Challenges are barriers or impediments to scientific progress that, if
overcome, will result in significant advances in biomedical knowledge.
There are 139 Compelling Questions and Critical Challenges outlined in the Strategic Vision. 
Approximately 110 are adjusted from the 2016 NHLBI Strategic Vision and 29 are new areas 
of inquiry. 
In the pages that follow, we dive more deeply into the eight objectives, explain their importance, 
and propose how pursuing them has the potential to reduce the public health burden of HLBS 
diseases and disorders.

26       NHLBI STRATEGIC VISION   |    FY 2026–2030
OBJECTIVE 1 •  Understand normal biological function and resilience  
Understanding normal biology is the backbone of all biomedical science. It is essential to 
understanding how the internal body keeps itself stable, predicting how biological systems 
respond to their environment, and recognizing disease pathways and targets for intervention. 
Research on normal biological function — including topics such as circadian rhythms, the 
microbiome, and tissue development from progenitor cells — can help us better define health  
and understand the earliest origins of disease processes. The scope of research on normal biology 
ranges from single cell analytics to studies of entire healthy populations. Using gold standard 
and emerging tools, methodologies, and technologies, such research can uncover the biological 
factors, behaviors, lifestyle factors, social circumstances, and environmental exposures that help 
people become resilient, which they must be to stay well as they age, experience stress, and 
endure adversity. Gaining new knowledge about the body’s intrinsic capacity to repair itself will 
yield greater insight into the transition from health to disease. For these reasons, understanding 
normal biology must remain a cornerstone of NHLBI-funded research.
ENVISION A FUTURE IN WHICH WE CAN
• Pr omote resilience and healthy aging through the application of regenerative strategies
using cells (e.g., progenitor cells) that enable the repair of HLBS systems.
• Characterize the molecular signatures of healthy heart, lung, and blood systems across
the lifespan, and develop early warning systems for molecular perturbations that lead
to disease.
• Pursue integrative analysis of large-scale data to characterize the molecular signature
of the heart, blood, lung, and blood systems that sustain health and wellness. This
data can include information derived from longitudinal electronic health records [EHR],
imaging and functional tests, and multiomics by emerging systems biology, artificial
intelligence, and machine learning.
• Understand how weather, and environmental exposures, social, environmental
exposures, social determinants, behaviors (e.g., diet and physical activity), and genetic
factors modulate biological systems, such as the epigenome, microbiome, and immune
systems, to sustain health and promote resilience.
NORMAL BIOLOGY

OBJECTIVE 2 •  Investigate newly discovered pathobiological mechanisms important  
to the onset and progression of heart, lung, and blood diseases and sleep disorders   
Discovering new pathobiological mechanisms and understanding them is critical to improving HLBS 
health. Such discoveries and research can potentially lead to clinical and implementation studies, 
which in turn can inform new therapeutic strategies and clinical practice. Important areas to focus 
on, with the help of emerging technologies such as molecular imaging and nanotechnology, include 
mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of rare and common diseases, disease-related structural 
and functional changes, and the clinical significance of these changes. In addition, tracking disease 
onset and progression across the lifespan is essential because it has the potential to inform 
our understanding of how chronic conditions become acute disease and how early exposures 
(environmental, etc.) and interventions, including lifestyle changes, impact health. 
ENVISION A FUTURE IN WHICH WE CAN
• Pr eempt the transition from health to disease and enable disease prevention through
an enhanced understanding of the pathobiological mechanisms underpinning the early
onset of heart, lung, and blood diseases and sleep disorders.
• Leverage high-throughput multiomics and other advanced technologies for deep
phenotyping in longitudinal cohort studies to define the functional significance of genetic
and epigenetic variants on human pathobiology, as well as their impact on clinical outcomes
involving heart, lung, and blood diseases and sleep disorders across the lifespan.
• Gain new insights into modifier genes and molecular pathways that influence the
variable clinical manifestations and outcomes of monogenic disorders (e.g., sickle
cell disease and cystic fibrosis) and structural defects (e.g., congenital heart disease),
thereby catalyzing new tailored therapeutic strategies.
• Identify commonalities underlying disparate heart, lung, and blood diseases and sleep
disorders to understand shared pathways and to identify shared therapeutic targets.
• Leverage emerging human complex tissue and three-dimensional cellular systems
to model the pathobiological processes and to identify targetable molecular/cellular
pathways that drive the onset and progression of heart, lung, and blood diseases and
sleep disorders.

OBJECTIVE 3 • Investigate factors that account for differences in health status  
among populations
Variations exist between populations — grouped by factors such as age, sex, race, and ancestry—
in susceptibility and resilience to heart, lung, and blood diseases and disorders as well as in 
disease course and outcomes. Although some of these variations are caused by genetic and 
other biological factors, a wide range of environmental and behavioral factors and socioeconomic 
inequities also contribute to health disparities. Research is needed to better understand the 
causes of population health differences and to identify strategies to effectively address them. 
Investigations in this area may range from basic laboratory studies to environmental and 
population science to community-centered implementation research.
ENVISION A FUTURE IN WHICH WE CAN
• Lev erage a deeper understanding of biologic differences related to sex or ancestral
groups (e.g., variation in ancestry leading to differences in asthma phenotypes among
ethnic subgroups) to devise more precise, targeted intervention strategies and to
further improve clinical outcomes.
• Leverage epidemiology and the power of data science, artificial intelligence, and
machine learning to understand and reduce sex-, race-, ethnicity-, and location-related
health disparities.
• Incorporate measures of diet and nutrition inequities, and health disparities in research
on heart, lung, and blood disease and sleep disorders across the lifespan, using
existing longitudinal cohorts, innovative designs for collecting exposure data, big data
approaches, individual biospecimens, and imaging using
remote digital technologies.

OBJECTIVE 4 • Identify factors that account for individual differences in pathobiology 
and in response to treatments 
Research advances in areas such as genomics and other “omics” (e.g., proteomics, metabolomics) 
have provided new opportunities to deepen our understanding of HLBS pathobiological processes 
and how they vary among individual patients by sex and other factors. Accelerating progress 
toward precise, individualized prevention efforts and medical interventions will require research 
into biological factors, environmental exposures, behavioral factors, and other influences that 
account for differences in pathobiology and unique responses to treatment (including drug 
reactions and other adverse events). This research will allow personal and clinical decisions, 
practices, and medical products to be tailored to the individual patient to help produce the best 
possible outcomes.
ENVISION A FUTURE IN WHICH WE CAN
• Dev elop precise clinical interventions across the lifespan by sex and based on
an individual’s environmental exposures, behaviors, genotypes, and
molecular-cellular phenotypes.
• Accelerate the incorporation of new imaging, omics, and sensor technologies with
advanced data analytics to inform a more precise clinical classification of chronic
diseases and acute conditions (e.g., asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, chronic obstructive
lung disease, heart failure, myocardial infarction), and enable more accurate diagnosis
and treatment.
• Develop and define individual HLBS health signatures by integrating all reliable and
available data (e.g., genome-wide association studies (GWAS), multiomics, genetic and
non-genetic information, social/environmental factors) to guide personalized prevention
strategies and clinical interventions.

OBJECTIVE 5 • Develop and optimize novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies  
to prevent, treat, and cure heart, lung, and blood diseases and sleep disorders
Recent scientific and technological developments offer especially promising opportunities 
to prevent disease, manage and treat illness, and promote resilience. These wide-ranging 
developments include new gene editing techniques to safely treat and prevent HLBS diseases  
and disorders, smart tools that monitor and adjust biological processes, techniques that  
modulate stem cell or immune system signaling to reduce disease risk, and advances in  
materials science that could yield vastly improved implant devices. Other technologies and 
bioengineering developments may further facilitate diagnostic capabilities. New lifestyle 
interventions may improve the maintenance of continued health and wellness and may enable 
behavioral modification to prevent disease. Many of these advances, which are the results of  
past investments in basic research, are crucial to developing and optimizing novel diagnostics  
and therapeutics strategies.   
ENVISION A FUTURE IN WHICH WE CAN
• Dev elop surgical grafts (using stem cells, 3D printing, and nanotechnologies) for
children born with heart defects, in which the grafts grow and adapt into adulthood,
making multiple operations unnecessary.
• Transform the safety and availability of the nation’s blood supply by using genetically
engineered stem cells to eliminate histoincompatible antigens and generate universal
donor red blood cells that are available off the shelf by a high-throughput process.
• Build intelligent health systems for HLBS diseases and disorders that use artificial
intelligence and machine learning tools that can screen patients for risk factors
for early disease development and that can diagnose and evaluate the effects of
interventions and treatments.
• Create biomimetic platforms that promote lung tissue regrowth, regeneration, repair,
and replacement of a patient’s individual lung cells and/or tissues to reduce the burden
of underlying lung diseases.

OBJECTIVE 6 • Optimize clinical and implementation research to improve health 
and reduce disease
For maximum return on NHLBI investments in research and research training, it is important 
to prioritize strategies that support integration of evidence-based interventions within clinical 
and public health settings. New methodologies, research frameworks, and resources must be 
developed to refine the conduct of clinical studies and implementation research, while also

NIA Strategic Directions 2020 1 
From the Director 
I am pleased to present the strategic directions of the National Institute on Aging (NIA) for 
2020-2025.  
Today, there are more Americans ages 65 and older — just over 49 million, according to the 
U.S. Census — than at any other time in history, and we expect these numbers to grow as more 
Baby Boomers (individuals born between 1946 and 1964) reach retirement age. We can 
attribute this unprecedented demographic shift to a variety of factors, many of which benefit 
people of all ages. For example, even within the lifetimes of today’s older Americans, infectious 
diseases that once cut millions of lives short have been largely controlled in the U.S., and public 
health campaigns and policy changes — for example, smoking cessation efforts and laws 
mandating seat belt use — have saved many more lives.  
Despite these advances, aging itself remains the most significant risk factor for many chronic 
diseases and conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease and related forms of dementia 
(AD/ADRD), most types of cancer, many types of heart disease, osteoporosis and hip fracture, 
kidney failure, and diabetes. While these diseases are rarely inevitable, it is probable that as the 
number of older Americans increases, so too will the number of people with age-related 
diseases. A significant increase in the number of individuals with serious chronic conditions will 
have profound social and economic effects on the nation. 
NIA is meeting these challenges through its ongoing mission to:  
• Support and conduct genetic, biological, clinical, behavioral, social, and economic 
research on aging. 
• Foster the development of research and clinician scientists in aging. 
• Provide research resources. 
• Disseminate information about aging and advances in research to the public, health care 
professionals, and the scientific community, among a variety of audiences. 
Our primary activities include funding extramural research at universities and research centers 
across the U.S. and around the world; maintaining an active communications and outreach 
program; and conducting a vibrant intramural research program at NIA laboratories in 
Baltimore and Bethesda, Maryland. In addition, as the lead federal agency for research on 
AD/ADRD, NIA has received an unprecedented influx of funding targeted toward understanding 
and addressing these conditions over the past seven years, and our plans and priorities reflect 
this extraordinary opportunity for discovery. 
This document presents our scientific priorities for the next five years. Consistent with guidance 
in the 21st Century Cures Act, we also lay out our goals and objectives with respect to some of 
the “behind the scenes” activities we conduct in order to support the science. It is our hope 
that this description of our priorities is useful to you, whether you’re an independent 
researcher, an advocate, or an interested layperson. 
For up-to-date information about NIA’s activities, priorities, and advances, I invite you to visit 
our web site at www.nia.nih.gov. 
Sincerely, 
Richard J. Hodes, M.D.
